title: Databricks
note: Databricks as durable design concepts: planes and cost, tables and layout, governance, incremental engineering, serving, and the Fabric decision. Product names and feature status are as of Nov 2026; menus, limits and new AI features live in the official docs. Refresh quarterly.

concepts.s: Databricks is three ideas plus a meter: a control plane governing compute over your data, tables that are files plus a transaction log under Unity Catalog, and declarative pipelines and jobs defined as code; DBUs meter all of it.

x.b:
• Planes and governance: Databricks runs the control plane; compute runs in your cloud (classic) or Databricks' fleet (serverless). Unity Catalog governs every table, file, model and function.
  • Tables: Parquet files plus a Delta (or Iceberg) log give ACID writes, time travel and layout management.
  • Pipelines as code: declarative pipelines, Lakeflow Jobs and bundles deploy the same definitions to dev, test and prod.
  • Meter: DBUs per SKU, queryable in system tables.
Trap: Learning product names instead of the three ideas. Names change yearly (DLT became Lakeflow pipelines; Asset Bundles became Declarative Automation Bundles in 2026).
"Why did spend jump?" is a meter question (system.billing), "who can read PHI?" a governance question (Unity Catalog), "why did prod drift from dev?" a pipelines-as-code question.

cards.q: A job in prod behaves differently from dev. Which of the three ideas do you check?
cards.a: Pipelines as code: is prod deployed from the same bundle definition, with only target settings differing?

cards.q: Where do you answer "which team drove last month's DBU spike"?
cards.a: The billing system tables (system.billing.usage) joined to tags.

concepts.s: Pick compute by workload: serverless by default for jobs, notebooks and SQL, classic job clusters when you need custom networking or images, and never interactive clusters for production.

x.b:
• Account: identities, metastores, billing. Workspace: where notebooks, jobs and dashboards live, attached to one metastore per region.
  • Serverless: no cluster config, fast start, Databricks-managed; the recommended default (as of Nov 2026).
  • Classic all-purpose clusters are for interactive work and bill at a higher rate than job clusters.
  • Access mode standard (multi-user, Unity Catalog isolation) suits most workloads; dedicated is for single users or groups.
  • Photon is the vectorized engine for SQL and DataFrame work.
Trap: Running scheduled jobs on an all-purpose cluster: higher rate, and it idles between runs.
Nightly pipeline: serverless job. Ad hoc exploration: a small all-purpose cluster with auto-termination at 30 minutes.

cards.q: A scheduled job runs on an all-purpose cluster. Why change it?
cards.a: Job compute (or serverless) bills at a lower rate and doesn't idle between runs.

cards.q: When might you still choose classic compute over serverless?
cards.a: When you need custom networking, images or libraries serverless doesn't support in your region.

concepts.s: Spend is DBUs per SKU (plus cloud VMs on classic), so tag everything, query the billing system tables, and fix layout and compute choice before buying more.

x.b:
• system.billing.usage holds every usage record with SKU, quantity and tags; join system.billing.list_prices for cost.
  • Tags on clusters, warehouses and jobs flow into billing; serverless uses usage policies for attribution.
  • Budgets alert on spend.
  • Biggest levers: serverless or job compute instead of all-purpose, auto-stop, incremental processing, good layout, right-sized warehouses.

Trap: Untagged serverless usage nobody can attribute.
Trap: Tuning cluster size before checking the query profile; most waste is scans and shuffles.

SELECT custom_tags['team'] AS team, SUM(usage_quantity) AS dbus
FROM system.billing.usage
WHERE usage_unit = 'DBU' AND usage_date >= current_date() - 30
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC

cards.q: Serverless spend can't be traced to teams. What fixes attribution?
cards.a: Serverless usage policies (and tags), so usage records carry team metadata.

cards.q: A warehouse is slow and expensive. What do you inspect before resizing?
cards.a: The query profile: scans, pruning, shuffles and spill.

concepts.s: Use Unity Catalog managed tables so the platform owns layout and maintenance, cluster with liquid clustering instead of partitions, and let predictive optimization compact and vacuum.

x.b:
• Managed tables: Unity Catalog controls path and lifecycle; managed-only features include predictive optimization and automatic liquid clustering. External: you own the files.
  • Delta: ACID, time travel, MERGE, deletion vectors.
  • Liquid clustering (CLUSTER BY, or CLUSTER BY AUTO) replaces partitioning and Z-order and is maintained incrementally.
  • Predictive optimization runs OPTIMIZE, VACUUM and ANALYZE on managed tables.
  • Iceberg: managed Iceberg tables and UniForm let Iceberg engines read the same data.

Trap: Hand-built partitioning on high-cardinality columns: small files and slow scans.
Trap: Changing clustering keys and expecting old data to move; that needs OPTIMIZE FULL.
CREATE TABLE silver.encounters (...) CLUSTER BY (clinic_id, event_date);

cards.q: A new table is filtered by clinic and date. Partition or cluster?
cards.a: Liquid clustering on (clinic_id, event_date); partitioning risks small files and can't evolve.

cards.q: You changed clustering keys but old data didn't reorganize. Why?
cards.a: Clustering is incremental; rewriting existing data needs OPTIMIZE FULL.

concepts.s: Unity Catalog is a catalog, schema, object hierarchy where grants on a parent are inherited below it, so grant to groups at the highest level that is still least privilege.

x.b:
• Metastore (one per region), then catalog, schema, then tables, views, volumes, functions and models.
  • Reading a table needs USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA and SELECT; writing needs MODIFY.
  • BROWSE exposes metadata without data. Ownership confers full control.
  • Every access path is checked and audited against the grants.

Trap: Granting to individuals: access becomes unreviewable. Grant to groups.
Trap: Granting SELECT on a catalog when one schema was meant: inheritance includes future tables.

GRANT USE CATALOG ON CATALOG clinical TO `analysts`;
GRANT USE SCHEMA, SELECT ON SCHEMA clinical.gold TO `analysts`;

cards.q: A user has SELECT on a table but still gets access denied. What is likely missing?
cards.a: USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA on the parents.

cards.q: Why is granting SELECT at catalog level risky?
cards.a: It is inherited by every current and future table in the catalog.

concepts.s: Protect sensitive rows and columns with SQL functions attached as row filters and column masks, and at scale with tag-driven ABAC policies that apply them to every matching table.

x.b:
• Row filter: a boolean function per table. Column mask: a function returning the value or a masked version, usually checking is_account_group_member().
  • Governed tags mark sensitive columns (for example phi). ABAC policies (GA 2026) apply filters and masks wherever the tags match, including new tables.
  • Data classification can detect and tag PII automatically.
Trap: Masking per table by hand: the next new table with MRNs ships unmasked. Tag-driven policies close that gap.
Tag MRN columns phi; one policy masks them for everyone except care-operations, across every current and future table.

cards.q: New tables keep shipping with unmasked MRNs. What structural fix?
cards.a: Governed tags plus an ABAC column-mask policy that applies to every tagged column automatically.

cards.q: What function typically drives a column mask's decision?
cards.a: A group-membership check such as is_account_group_member().

concepts.s: For HIPAA data, enable the compliance security profile on the workspace, and use system tables for audit, lineage and access review.

x.b:
• The compliance security profile (HIPAA standard) adds hardened images, automatic cluster updates, enhanced monitoring and TLS requirements, at added cost. Check which serverless products it covers in your region.
  • A BAA covers it: with Databricks on AWS and GCP, with Microsoft on Azure Databricks. You stay responsible for your own controls.
  • System tables: access.audit for who did what, table and column lineage, query history. Retention as of Nov 2026: about 395 days for audit and lineage, 365 for query history, billing indefinitely.
Trap: Assuming every serverless product is covered by the profile in every region. Check before routing PHI.
Quarterly access review: query system.access.audit for reads on tagged PHI tables by principal, and compare with approved roles.

cards.q: What must be on before a Databricks workspace processes HIPAA data?
cards.a: The compliance security profile with the HIPAA standard (plus a BAA).

cards.q: Where do you prove who read a PHI table last quarter?
cards.a: The audit system table (system.access.audit).

concepts.s: Query external databases in place with Lakehouse Federation, share live read-only data across organizations with OpenSharing, and use clean rooms when parties must combine data without seeing each other's rows.

x.b:
• Lakehouse Federation: a connection plus foreign catalog exposes SQL Server, PostgreSQL, Snowflake, OneLake (read-only, Azure) and others under Unity Catalog grants, pushing queries down where possible. Best for exploration and migration.
  • OpenSharing (Delta Sharing renamed and extended, June 2026; existing clients still work): live read-only tables, views, models and more, Databricks-to-Databricks without tokens or to other platforms with tokens or OIDC.
  • Clean rooms: approved code runs on combined data; outputs go to output tables.

Trap: Dashboards pointed at federated operational databases: every refresh hits the source system. Ingest for heavy, repeated analytics.
Trap: Tables with table-level row filters or masks can't be shared; share a dynamic view or a de-identified copy. ABAC-masked tables can be shared only if the share owner is exempt, so recipients see unmasked data.
During migration, federate the on-prem SQL Server warehouse to validate new tables against it, then cut over to ingested tables.

cards.q: A dashboard over a federated SQL Server database slows the source. Fix?
cards.a: Ingest the data (Lakeflow Connect) instead of querying it in place on every refresh.

cards.q: How do you share a table that has table-level column masks?
cards.a: Share a dynamic view or a de-identified copy; the masked table itself can't be shared.

concepts.s: Ingest with tools that track what they have processed: Lakeflow Connect for databases and SaaS apps, Auto Loader for files, each resuming from a checkpoint.

x.b:
• Lakeflow Connect: managed connectors (SQL Server CDC, Salesforce, Workday and more) writing streaming tables; CDC database connectors run an always-on ingestion gateway on classic compute, billed even when idle.
  • Auto Loader (cloudFiles): exactly-once file ingestion, schema inference and evolution, unexpected fields in _rescued_data; file events beat directory listing at scale.
  • Triggers: availableNow for cheap batch-like runs, processingTime for continuous micro-batches.
  • Change data feed exposes row-level changes downstream.
Trap: Deleting or sharing a checkpoint between streams: the stream reprocesses or skips data.

spark.readStream.format("cloudFiles")
  .option("cloudFiles.format", "json")
  .option("cloudFiles.schemaLocation", "/Volumes/.../schema")
  .load(path).writeStream.trigger(availableNow=True)...

cards.q: A file-ingestion stream should run hourly and stop when done. Which trigger?
cards.a: availableNow=True: process everything new, then stop.

cards.q: Where do unexpected fields land with Auto Loader schema evolution?
cards.a: In the _rescued_data column.

concepts.s: Declare streaming tables and materialized views and let the engine infer dependencies, manage checkpoints, enforce expectations and apply CDC.

x.b:
• Lakeflow pipelines (formerly DLT, built on Spark Declarative Pipelines): streaming tables process each input once; materialized views refresh incrementally when possible.
  • Expectations: CONSTRAINT ... EXPECT with warn, drop or fail on violation, recorded in the event log.
  • AUTO CDC applies change feeds with ordering and SCD Type 1 or 2.

Trap: Expectations set to warn everywhere: bad data flows and nobody looks at the log.
Trap: Full refreshes of streaming tables that discard history the source no longer has.

CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE silver_encounters (
  CONSTRAINT valid_id EXPECT (encounter_id IS NOT NULL) ON VIOLATION DROP ROW
) AS SELECT * FROM STREAM(bronze_encounters);

cards.q: Rows with null keys must never reach silver but the pipeline should keep running. Which expectation action?
cards.a: ON VIOLATION DROP ROW (tracked in the event log).

cards.q: What does AUTO CDC handle that a hand-written MERGE often gets wrong?
cards.a: Out-of-order changes, by sequencing on a column, plus SCD Type 1 or 2 history.

concepts.s: Orchestrate with Lakeflow Jobs and define jobs, pipelines and dashboards in bundles, so the same reviewed YAML deploys to every environment.

x.b:
• Jobs: task DAGs with run-if conditions, if/else and for-each, and triggers on schedule, file arrival or table update; repair runs rerun only unsuccessful tasks and their dependents.
  • Bundles (Declarative Automation Bundles, formerly Asset Bundles): databricks.yml with targets; bundle validate, plan, deploy -t prod.
  • Deploy prod from CI as a service principal.

Trap: Editing prod jobs in the UI: the next bundle deploy reverts them.
Trap: Cron schedules racing upstream data; use table-update triggers.

databricks bundle validate
databricks bundle deploy -t prod   # from CI, as a service principal

cards.q: A gold job sometimes runs before silver finishes. Which trigger fixes it?
cards.a: A table-update trigger on the silver table instead of a cron schedule.

cards.q: One task in a 12-task job failed. How do you rerun efficiently?
cards.a: A repair run, which reruns only the failed and dependent tasks.

concepts.s: Serve BI from serverless SQL warehouses, define KPIs once as metric views, and diagnose slow queries with the query profile before resizing.

x.b:
• Serverless warehouses start in seconds and include Photon; size sets per-cluster power, min and max clusters set concurrency, auto-stop ends idle cost.
  • Metric views: measures and dimensions defined once in YAML as Unity Catalog objects, queried with MEASURE() at any grain.
  • Power BI connects to warehouses or gets semantic models published from Unity Catalog; Genie offers natural-language Q and A over curated data.
Trap: Scaling warehouse size for concurrency. Size speeds single queries; more clusters serve more users.
Monday-morning dashboard queuing: raise max clusters from 1 to 3, keep size; check query history for queue time versus run time.

cards.q: Dashboards queue when many users log in, but single queries are fast. What do you change?
cards.a: Max clusters (scale-out for concurrency), not warehouse size.

cards.q: How do metric views keep KPI definitions consistent?
cards.a: Each measure is defined once as a governed object and computed correctly at any grain with MEASURE().

concepts.s: Choose Import or DirectQuery by freshness, cost and security: Import caches data under the refresh identity, so Unity Catalog row filters and masks stop protecting report viewers.

x.b:
• Power BI connects to a SQL warehouse; Databricks can publish Unity Catalog tables as a semantic model, and a Lakeflow Jobs Power BI task (preview) can refresh it after the tables build.
  • Import: fastest visuals; refresh cost and latency follow the schedule; row-level security must be rebuilt in Power BI.
  • DirectQuery with per-user SSO: fresh data, Unity Catalog filters and masks apply per query, but warehouse cost and latency scale with users.
  • Dual mode for dimensions; aggregation tables or materialized views to cut DirectQuery load.
Trap: Import over PHI tables with a service principal: everyone sees what the refresh identity saw. Use Power BI RLS or DirectQuery with SSO.
A clinic-scoped PHI report: DirectQuery with SSO so Unity Catalog row filters apply per viewer; the KPI dashboard: Import on de-identified aggregates.
Which semantic layer is authoritative: Power BI DAX or Databricks metric views?

cards.q: An Import-mode report over masked PHI shows unmasked data to viewers. Why?
cards.a: Import caches data as the refresh identity saw it; Unity Catalog masks apply only at refresh.

cards.q: Why orchestrate the model refresh from the Lakeflow job?
cards.a: So refresh never runs on half-loaded tables.

concepts.s: Both store open Delta data and serve Power BI; choose by pricing model, governance, engineering depth and operating model, and expect to integrate rather than replace.

x.b:
• Pricing: Databricks bills consumption (DBUs); Fabric bills a shared capacity with smoothing and throttling.
  • Governance: Unity Catalog versus workspace roles, OneLake security and Purview.
  • Engineering: Databricks is deeper on Spark, streaming, pipelines and ML; Fabric bundles Data Factory, a T-SQL warehouse and real-time intelligence.
  • BI: Fabric is Power BI's home (Direct Lake).
  • Integration: Fabric can mirror Unity Catalog, and Unity Catalog tables in OneLake are in Beta.
Trap: Choosing on feature checklists. The real differences are cost shape, governance model and team skills.
Heavy streaming and ML engineering: Databricks for engineering, Fabric or Power BI for consumption, joined by mirroring.
Is spend spiky (favors consumption) or steady (favors capacity)?

cards.q: Workloads are spiky with long idle periods. Which pricing model fits better?
cards.a: Consumption (Databricks DBUs) over a fixed shared capacity.

cards.q: What is Fabric's main structural advantage for Power BI-heavy shops?
cards.a: It's Power BI's home, with Direct Lake over OneLake.
